newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania c.bank tries to lure funds back to banks.
newsitem.headline: Albania c.bank tries to lure funds back to banks.

text.p: Albania's central bank governor said on Monday the bank had raised interest rates on deposits to attract money back into the banking system following the collapse of high-interest pyramid investment schemes.
Qamil Tusha told Reuters the bank, whose foreign exchange reserves of $230 million had remained intact through the crisis, was following policies aimed at stabilising the monetary system.

He said the budget deficit of about 20 percent of gross domestic product was putting strong pressure on the lek, but he was satisfied with an exchange rate of 175 to 185 to the dollar in view of the deficit and the increase in banknote emission.
The lek started the year at 100 to the dollar and was quoted at 177 on the street market on Monday.

Tusha said the central bank had increased interest rates on three-month deposits to 37 percent to attract money back into the banking system, which had lost two billion leks in the crisis, including 1.2 billion in cash looted from banks in riots following the pyramid schemes' collapse.
Rates on one-year deposits were 32 percent.

"Deposits are increasing, people are turning back to the banks," said Tusha who was appointed in April after President Sali Berisha sacked the previous governor Kristaq Luniku who fled Albania at the height of the violence in February.
He said the combined reserves of the three state-owned commercial banks had fallen to 500 million leks. Albania hoped to privatise two of them.
He said he expected inflation to reach 50 percent by year end, compared to 17.4 percent in 1996. Other forecasts have put the 1997 figure at 70 percent.

He said central bank foreign exchange reserves of $230 million were enough to cover three months' imports and had not been touched in intervention at the end of May when the bank sold $2 million to bring the lek back from a low of 194.
"We're following a stabilisation policy now and I think with a new cabinet and a new economic programme we would like to draw up a suitable monetary programme," Tusha said.
He said the country would initially rely on balance of payments support from the International Monetary Fund and other creditors to get the recovery under way.
Alarmed at the crisis in Europe's poorest country which sent thousands of refugees fleeing to Italy and Greece, Western countries are keen to offer technical and financial help.

Diplomats say the international financial institutions have made the winding up of remaining high interest investment schemes a precondition for any new lending, to prevent funds being used to compensate savers or even fuel new pyramids.

The Socialist Party, which will have a more than two-thirds majority in the new parliament, has promised to compensate investors as much as possible, and to ensure transparency. Foreign auditors are expected to be appointed to liquidate the remaining schemes and recover what assets are left.

Tusha said two of the five collapsed schemes had already been wound up. Investors had received about half their money back from the Populli and Xhafferi schemes, and some 35 percent of that had been deposited in banks, he said.

The funds flourished after the fall of communism in 1990 as new companies scrambled for cash that the tiny banking system could not supply. While some were genuine investment funds building up businesses, others were pure pyramids taking money from new investors to pay the old.
Drafting legislation to control investment funds will be one of the first tasks of the new government. Previous efforts fell prey to pre-election political bickering.
